title: Population Pyramids
meta_desc: A-Level Geography adventure on population pyramids, dependency ratio and stage identification.

walkthroughs.body_html: Stage 2: classic pyramid (wide base, narrow top); Niger today. Stage 3: narrowing base; India transitioning. Stage 4: stable rectangular (UK, USA). Stage 5: inverted pyramid (Japan, Germany). Shape reveals fertility history, mortality patterns, migration.

Youthful: Niger dependency ratio 113 (50 percent under 15); high education and healthcare burden. UK ratio 58 (rising as boomers age). Japan 71 with elderly burden. Economic productivity hindered when workers support many non-workers either young or old.

Bulge of working-age population with falling fertility creates dividend. East Asian Tigers (Korea, Taiwan, Singapore) captured this 1960-2000 via education + jobs. India enters dividend now (working-age 67 percent of population) but needs to create 12 million jobs/yr to capture it.

mcqs.q: What happens in Stage 2 of the Demographic Transition Model?
options: Birth rates rise rapidly because people want larger families.
Both birth and death rates fall sharply in Stage 2.
Death rates fall rapidly (due to better food, sanitation and medicine) while birth rates remain high, causing rapid population growth.
The DTM only applies to countries with more than 50 million people.

mcqs.q: Why is the Demographic Transition Model criticised for not applying to all countries?
options: It was based on European industrialisation. LICs today face different conditions: imported medicine without industrialisation, cultural factors, gender inequality and globalised economies — not all follow the same path.
The DTM only applies to countries with more than 50 million people.
Both birth and death rates fall sharply in Stage 2.
All countries follow the five stages of the DTM in order.

mcqs.q: How is the dependency ratio calculated?
options: Both birth and death rates fall sharply in Stage 2.
The dependency ratio is the number of children per family.
(Population aged 0-14 plus population aged 65+) divided by population aged 15-64, multiplied by 100 — comparing dependants to the working-age population.
The dependency ratio is the number of unemployed people in a country.
